 Lawsuit challenges Virginia reproductive rights amendment ahead of Election Day
 A Bedford County supervisor is appealing a dismissed lawsuit that argues state lawmakers failed to follow required procedures before placing the reproductive rights amendment on the November ballot.
 Jocelyn Routt , Community Journalist
 Published:  October 26, 2026 at 6:04 PM Tags:  Virginia Reproductive Rights , Election , Election Day , Lawsuit , Challenge , Bedford County , Bedford County Supervisor BEDFORD CO., Va. – A legal challenge could affect the future of Virginia’s proposed reproductive rights constitutional amendment, even after voters cast their ballots.
 Bedford County Supervisor Charla Bansley is challenging the process used to place Question 1 on the November 3 ballot. The lawsuit argues state officials failed to follow required procedures for proposing a constitutional amendment.
 Mat Staver, founder and chairman of Liberty Counsel, which represents Bansley, said the process did not follow the necessary rules.
 “The procedures were not followed intentionally in this case,” Staver said.
 What is the lawsuit challenging?
 The lawsuit focuses on whether lawmakers followed the proper legal process — not on how many voters support or oppose the amendment.
 Staver argues the proposed amendment’s language should have been made public at least 90 days before the 2025 House of Delegates election. He says that requirement gives voters an opportunity to understand a proposed constitutional change and hold lawmakers accountable.
 The case was dismissed in circuit court, and Bansley appealed. The Virginia Court of Appeals is reviewing the challenge.
 Aaron S. Van Allen, department chair and associate professor of government at Liberty University, said the court will need to examine whether lawmakers followed the appropriate procedures and timeline.
 “Did the General Assembly follow the appropriate timetable? Did they follow the appropriate protocols in order to get for the question to even end up on the ballot?” Van Allen said.
 What does Question 1 mean for Virginia voters?
 Question 1 asks voters whether to amend the Virginia Constitution to protect reproductive freedom, including decisions involving prenatal care, childbirth, contraception, abortion, miscarriage management and fertility care.
 The proposed amendment would also protect patients and providers from certain penalties related to reproductive decisions. It would allow the state to regulate abortion during the third trimester, with exceptions involving the pregnant patient’s health and fetal viability.
 Read the official Question 1 ballot language from the Virginia Department of Elections .
 Van Allen emphasized that challenging the process used to put an amendment on the ballot is different from challenging the amendment’s actual language.
 “One is what we would say is looking at the merits of the language itself. The other one is more of a procedural motion,” Van Allen said.
 Could the courts overturn the amendment after the election?
 The legal challenge could continue after Election Day, meaning the final outcome of the vote may not settle the amendment’s future.
 Staver argues the amendment should be invalidated regardless of whether voters approve or reject it. That is the plaintiff’s position, not a final court ruling.
 Van Allen said voters should still make their decisions based on their own values and interests while the legal process continues.
 The case is now before the Virginia Court of Appeals. Its outcome will determine what happens next in the legal challenge.
